live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37, ScarCruft): a long-running espionage actor focused on Korea
next.in_short: NICKEL FOXCROFT, better known as APT37 or ScarCruft, is described by several vendors as a North Korea-linked espionage group. Reports show it targeting South Korea-focused activists, officials and defectors with shortcut-file lures and…

sentences.t: The Secworks catalogue tracks NICKEL FOXCROFT under many other names, including APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, InkySquid, Group 123 and Venus 121.
CrowdStrike describes RICOCHET CHOLLIMA as a DPRK-nexus targeted intrusion adversary involved in espionage since at least 2016.
ESET says ScarCruft, also known as APT37 or Reaper, has operated since at least 2012 and is suspected to be a North Korean espionage group.

One analysis of the RokRat backdoor calls APT37 a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group. Another report says the exact relationship between the group and the North Korean state remains somewhat unclear.
Genians says some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group, because they overlap in targets and infrastructure. A cited MSMT report assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
CrowdStrike says its observed operations have almost exclusively targeted the Republic of Korea. It assesses the focus to be government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists.
AhnLab's ASEC team says the group goes after individuals such as human rights activists, reporters and North Korean defectors.
Genians reports a March 2025 spear phishing campaign aimed at activists focused on North Korea. The lures impersonated a South Korean national security think tank.
360 Advanced Threat Research Institute says a RokRat campaign targeted government personnel and corporations in South Korea and Asia.
ESET infers that a trojanized game platform mainly targeted ethnic Koreans in Yanbian, China, most likely refugees or defectors.
Phishing emails carrying malicious shortcut (LNK) files are a recurring entry point. The shortcut runs PowerShell, which loads the RokRat backdoor in memory.
RokRat uses legitimate cloud services such as pCloud, Yandex and Dropbox for command and control.
In early 2023, AhnLab saw the group exploit an old flaw in the Hangul word processor (CVE-2017-8291). The payload was hidden inside a JPEG image, and the chain installed a backdoor called M2RAT.

Zscaler describes a Windows shortcut or help-file chain that drops the Rust backdoor Rustonotto and the PowerShell backdoor Chinotto. A later stage delivers FadeStealer, which collects files, keystrokes, screenshots and audio.

ESET reports a supply-chain attack on a gaming platform, using trojanized Windows and Android components. Lookout attributes the KoSpy Android spyware to ScarCruft with medium confidence, noting that North Korean groups share infrastructure and techniques.
S2W judged, from analysis of tactics and tools, that a December 2020 watering-hole attack was related to ScarCruft. The final payload was a ROKRAT variant.
Lookout dates KoSpy samples from March 2022 to March 2024. The apps posed as utilities and were removed from Google Play.
ESET believes the game-platform attack was probably under way since late 2024.

Zscaler's Ruby Jumper report, published 26 February 2026, describes a campaign that spreads over removable media to reach air-gapped networks. It delivers tools including RESTLEAF, SNAKEDROPPER, THUMBSBD and BLUELIGHT.

Treat unexpected shortcut files inside archives with suspicion, especially if you work on Korea-related issues. Keep software patched and monitor PowerShell activity and traffic to cloud storage services.
